ON MARCH 18, FILM STUDIES MAJORS PRESENTED THEIR WORK AT ADLER AUDITORIUM.
Four short films created by students were screened, and each filmmaker answered questions from audience members. The films were striking in their variety. The program began with a whimsical animated film, Insides, depicting the internal organs of a human body interacting with one another like family members. Filmmaker Kat Morgan said the idea came to her while she was taking Human Anatomy 101. Next up was Alan Hinds' sober black-and-white documentary On My Feet, chronicling his brother's unsuccessful attempt to become a champion marathon runner. The third film in the series was Margot Bridges' comedy The Date, about a mismatched couple on a movie date.
And lastly, the audience saw The Friend, Priti Patel's tender depiction of a toddler's relationship with a protective dog. All four films were technically accomplished, engaging, and reflective of each filmmaker's distinctive, individual talents.

Stay Healthy During + Cold And Flu Season
Cases of flu have been climbing this winter, and the Campus Health Services office is advising all students, faculty, and staff to take precautions.
Campus Health Services offers free flu vaccinations and recommends that everyone except those with vaccine allergies come to get the quick and effective shot.
In addition, measures like handwashing can make a big difference in reducing your exposure to the flu virus. And of course, if you feel sick, avoid close contact with others to keep from spreading your illness.
Flu symptoms include fever, aches, sore throat, and fatigue. While these symptoms are also typical of the common cold, the flu tends to come on quite rapidly and symptoms can be severe. Students experiencing these symptoms should see one of the Health Services doctors as soon as possible. In some cases, antiviral medication may be prescribed.

The university has introduced a new housing program that provides affordable dormitories with modern amenities. Aimed at fostering a sense of community, these dormitories include common areas for socializing and studying.
In response to student feedback, the university has also expanded its campus employment opportunities, offering over 200 new positions in various departments. Additionally, Ridgeview is boosting its volunteering programs through partnerships with local nonprofit organizations, enabling students to earn credits while making a positive impact in the community. “Our goal is to create an environment where students can thrive academically and socially,” said Evan Carrow, Dean of Student Life.

CAMPUS RESEARCHERS "CRACK" THE CONCRETE CODE
Researchers at the university have developed an affordable self-healing concrete. When cracks form, embedded microcapsules release a gap-sealing mineral solution. The prototype has already survived 50 freeze-thaw cycles in the lab, and now real-world testing is beginning on campus walkways, although students and faculty probably will not notice anything unusual beneath their feet. Researchers predict huge benefits. "Our goal is to reduce costly repairs and extend building lifespans," said lead researcher Dr. Elena Vargas. "Imagine bridges that fix themselves after storms." Civil engineering professor Mark Chen called the innovation both practical and environmentally responsible. "This could revolutionize construction," he said. "By minimizing waste and extending the life of materials, we're saving money and reducing the environmental footprint." Larger trials are in the works, but for now campus walkways are a living laboratory, offering a glimpse into a future where concrete is resilient enough to heal itself.

Students were stunned when actor Daniel Rivero, famous for his award-winning role in Horizon's Edge, visited Ashburn College on Monday. He also praised Ashburn's faculty for fostering his love of storytelling. "It feels like I never left," he added. English 202: The Sonnet
The sonnet entered English literature in the early sixteenth century, adapted from the Italian form pioneered by Petrarch, and has inspired experimentation ever since. Poets writing in English have created endless variations on the basic formula of fourteen lines of rhymed verse in iambic pentameter. From the Renaissance to the modern era, poets have used the sonnet form to explore romantic, existential, and political themes in ways both serious and satiric. Because the sonnet is governed by strict formal rules, it is sometimes used to playfully illuminate the tension between constraint and creative freedom.
Readings will include sonnets by Sir Philip Sidney, William Shakespeare, John Donne, William Wordsworth, Claude McKay, Gwendolyn Brooks, Edna St. Vincent Millay, Cathy Park Hong, and Jericho Brown. Students will experiment with writing their own sonnets and will read them aloud in class. A final ten-page term paper will be due on May 15.

Time Capsule Unearthed During Dorm Renovation
Construction crews renovating Murdoch Hall have discovered a time capsule buried by students in the year 1896, sparking excitement across campus. Inside were letters, photographs, and a campus map showing buildings long gone. "It's like stepping into the past," said archivist Dana Wells, who catalogued the items. Students lined up to view the capsule's contents, marveling at the artifacts. "Seeing their hopes and dreams—it's inspiring," said junior Malik Johnson. The university will host an exhibit next month featuring the capsule's contents alongside reflections from current students, some of whom have expressed interest in contributing to a new capsule, creating a bridge between the past and the present. "It's a reminder of how much has changed—and how much hasn't," Wells added. The discovery has sparked conversations about campus traditions and the importance of preserving history, turning a routine renovation into a moment of shared pride and curiosity.

Student Housing Dilemma: A Shortage of Affordable Options
As the new academic year kicks off at Bridgeford University, students face significant challenges in finding places to live. Reports indicate a significant shortage of affordable on-campus accommodation, pushing many to seek alternatives in the already competitive off-campus market. Sarah Lee, a sophomore, notes, "Last year, I secured on-campus housing easily, but this time I had to move two miles away, turning a five-minute walk into a fifteen-minute drive." According to the university's Housing Department, this shortage is due to increased enrollment and delayed construction of new dormitories. The Student Union has stepped in, advocating for more immediate solutions like temporary housing subsidies and partnerships with local landlords. Additionally, the Union is organizing workshops on tenant rights and apartment-hunting strategies. Campus officials assure students that efforts are underway to accelerate dormitory construction, aiming for completion by next fall. Housing affordability is an issue that demands long-term solutions as university enrollment keeps rising.

Discover Estonia's Timeless Charm
Nestled in northern Europe, Estonia blends cultural heritage with natural beauty, making it a captivating destination. Its crown jewel, Tallinn's medieval Old Town—a UNESCO World Heritage site—invites visitors to wander cobblestone streets, admire historic buildings, and climb St. Olaf's Church for sweeping views. Town Hall Square buzzes with markets, offering a glimpse of vibrant local life. Just outside the capital, Lahemaa National Park showcases misty forests, tranquil bogs, and pristine coastlines. Adventurers can explore scenic trails and spot wildlife like moose and lynx. Off the coast, Kihnu Island preserves age-old traditions, where locals wear folk attire and celebrate with music and festivals, offering an authentic cultural experience. English is widely spoken, but learning a few Estonian phrases will enrich your journey. With its long daylight hours and mild weather, summer is the ideal season to explore Estonia's enchanting landscapes and living history.

visible_text: Yesterday, the university flipped the switch on its new nuclear research reactor in the basement of the Franklin Applied Energy Lab, turning the engineering quad into the hottest spot on campus—literally and figuratively. The reactor, about the size of a classroom, won't charge cell phones or brew coffee; it's built for neutron experiments, advanced materials research, and isotope production. "The launch of this laboratory will provide unparalleled opportunities for the university," said Dr. Evelyn Pillai, project lead. While some students have expressed safety concerns, a university spokesperson assured the community that the reactor is safer than the chemistry labs most first-year students wander into. "Radiation levels outside the facility are lower than what you'd get on a cross-country flight," said Dr. Pillai. Meanwhile, the Physics Club is planning a festive "Critical Mass Mixer" for Friday evening. The invitation features an atom whose colorful orbiting electrons are juggled by a mole.

Blackout Brings Creativity to Finals Week
A sudden power outage during finals week left Smithfield students scrambling for solutions. Students took advantage of their smart-phone flashlights, and university staff provided camping lights for dorm lounges. "It was stressful but kind of fun," said sophomore Grace Lee. The blackout lasted six hours, caused by a transformer failure near campus. Dining services offered free coffee, and professors extended deadlines to ease the pressure. "We made the best of it," said senior Omar Davis, who studied with his bike light. Social media buzzed with photos of candlelit study sessions, turning the inconvenience into a moment of campus unity. Some students even organized impromptu acoustic concerts on the quad, proving that creativity thrives under constraints. "It reminded us that community matters more than convenience," said Professor Laura Chen. By the early morning hours, power was restored, but the evening's events left a lasting impression.

CULN 310 Advanced Techniques: Sous Vide Course Description: This course explores the sous vide culinary method, a meticulous process in which vacuum-sealed pouches are placed in a water bath at a precisely controlled temperature. Students who successfully complete the course will be able to harness their knowledge of the biochemical interactions and thermal dynamics that underly the sous vide technique to achieve optimal flavor profiles and textural nuances. Successful students will also be able to demonstrate their understanding of the historical progression and contemporary adaptations of sous vide technology, engage with state-of-the-art sous vide equipment, and critically evaluate the applications of the sous vide technique in haute cuisine.
Prerequisites: CULN 110 (Foundational Culinary Arts) and CULN 153 (Introduction to Gastronomic Science). Enrollment is limited to Culinary Arts advanced track students.

visible_text: Kintsugi, an ancient Japanese art, transforms broken pottery into objects of beauty by highlighting, not hiding, their cracks. Artisans use lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum to repair fractures, creating pieces that often become more valued than their original form. Originating in the late fifteenth century, kintsugi reflects the philosophy of wabi-sabi, which honors imperfection and transience. Its message extends beyond ceramics, inspiring personal growth and resilience by advising people to embrace flaws as part of life’s narrative. Rather than viewing damage as failure, kintsugi reframes it as transformation, symbolizing strength, authenticity, and renewal in a perfection-driven world. Today, workshops and studios worldwide teach both its technical craft and its profound philosophy, offering learners not only artistic skills but insights into acceptance, individuality, and creative expression. Kintsugi stands as a timeless reminder that beauty lies in uniqueness and in the stories our “cracks” reveal, an idea that applies to academic life and beyond.

visible_text: The Rise of Sustainable Living in University Housing Martinsburg (April 10) As universities trend toward eco-consciousness, more students are embracing sustainable living in campus housing. At Greenleaf University, the new EcoHousing initiative features solar panels and rainwater-harvesting systems. Select dorms also have communal gardens. This program aligns with students’ growing demand for environmentally friendly spaces. In a recent survey, 78 percent of Greenleaf students expressed interest in sustainable housing. The initiative also includes workshops on recycling and energy conservation, aiming to create environmentally aware graduates. Emily Hart, a senior in environmental science, noted, “Living sustainably on campus shows that daily choices have global impact.” The administration hopes this program will inspire other schools to follow suit. Greenleaf even offers financial incentives: Students who choose EcoHousing receive a 5 percent discount on housing fees. The university plans to expand the initiative to more dorms next year.
